v.why: Replacing a missing direct input-to-output edge with skip gains much more (+2.8/+3.9/+16.5) than replacing a real conv or pool op (about -1 to +2 on C10/C100).
With edge 3 none, the output depends on edges 4 and 5, so adding a conv on edge 5 can reconnect the graph (+76/+64/+24 when edges 4 and 5 are also none).
Edge 1 becomes the main route to the output when edge 3 is none, and skip there gave +10 on IN16 versus about 0 to 3 otherwise.
Without the direct edge, strengthening edge 4 matters more (+1.5/+1.2/+8.9) than when edge 3 is already a conv (about -0.7 to +1.5).
A conv on edge 4 compensates for the missing direct path, giving +3.1/+0.9/+11.8 versus roughly 0 to 0.8 on C10/C100 otherwise.
Turning a removed edge 3 into a 3x3 conv gives a larger gain (+3.8/+6.5/+17.5) than upgrading an existing skip (+1.0/0.0/+3.7) or a conv1x1 (+2.8/+2.8/+8.7).
An existing skip on edge 3 already supplies a direct path, so upgrading it to conv3x3 adds less than upgrading a conv1x1 or avg_pool edge.
With edge 4 none, edge 5 is the only route from node 2 to the output besides edge 3, so replacing its conv with pooling costs more (-1.4/-2.0/-5.7).
Restoring a removed first edge to a conv3x3 gives the largest gain across all three datasets (+1.2/+2.3/+1.2) compared with replacing an existing 1x1 conv or skip.
Replacing a pooling op with a conv on edge 5 helps more (+1.4/+1.1/+4.4) than replacing a skip or conv1x1, where IN16 drops by 1 to 1.5.

raw:

I did not run any further experiments or checks beyond reading the logged results. Hypotheses 8 to 10 rest on thinner evidence (a handful of runs each) and are the least certain.
